name: Georges Bataille
role: French writer, philosopher and theorist of expenditure and sovereignty (1897–1962)
summary: Bataille combined revolutionary anticapitalism and antifascism with a critique of lives subordinated to production and utility. His later economic work favoured international redistribution and peaceful transformation, while his writing explored sacred experience and the limits of rational mastery.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: He preferred coordinated aid to profit-bound international lending.

public-ownership.rationale: His jointly led 1935 programme demanded immediate socialisation of major heavy industries.

property-fundamental.rationale: His programme subordinated private productive property to eventual collective ownership.

worker-ownership.rationale: The programme made collective producer ownership the foundation of a non-alienated society.

traditional-family.rationale: The Contre-Attaque tract he spoke at calls the family the foundation of social constraint, and his co-written note holds parental morality to be the base of capitalist social morality.

nation-first.rationale: He explicitly rejected the national perspective in evaluating global economic welfare.

revolution-justified.rationale: His 1935-36 Contre-Attaque texts called for armed revolution, but by 1949 (The Accursed Share) he looked to peaceful evolution; the later view does not settle this statement, so under the recency rule it is left null.

democracy-best.rationale: His early dictatorship programme contrasts with later hopes for American democracy’s peaceful success.

political-violence-never.rationale: His 1935-36 Contre-Attaque texts called for armed revolution, but by 1949 (The Accursed Share) he looked to peaceful evolution; the later view does not settle this statement, so under the recency rule it is left null.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The signed manifesto calls class struggle a historical factor and source of essential moral values, and his 1933 essay makes it central, but neither calls it the main driver of all history.

self-interest-moral.rationale: He contrasts an experience of generosity and expenditure with one dominated by selfishness and calls a world of self-interest and obligation to work hideous.

direct-action.rationale: His 1935-36 Contre-Attaque texts called for armed revolution, but by 1949 (The Accursed Share) he looked to peaceful evolution; the later view does not settle this statement, so under the recency rule it is left null.

means-match-ends.rationale: His programme proposed appropriating fascist techniques of fanatic mobilisation for universal emancipation.

distribute-by-need.rationale: He endorsed allocation according to need in international assistance.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: His 1935-36 Contre-Attaque texts called for armed revolution, but by 1949 (The Accursed Share) he looked to peaceful evolution; the later view does not settle this statement, so under the recency rule it is left null.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: He held that international economic contradictions could be resolved peacefully.

reason-over-faith.rationale: He rejected a life confined to reason and learning and valued experiences outside discursive knowledge, including laughter and ecstatic states.

class-collaboration.rationale: In 1933 he called the bourgeois efforts to better workers' lot a cowardly substitute and class struggle the grandest social expenditure; the manifesto he signed affirms class struggle.

workers-nation.rationale: The manifesto calls enclosing the revolution in the national frame of a dominating country timid and puts a universal revolution in its place.

state-class-instrument.rationale: His fascism essay explicitly linked the modern state’s protective function to bourgeois social organisation, while adding an account of sovereign authority.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: In 1935 he regretted the Popular Front's abandonment of revolutionary defeatism and warned of a new crusade of the democracies; his group's supplement was titled 'The Revolution or the War'.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: He testified for the defence of the publisher prosecuted for circulating Sade’s supposedly immoral books. This establishes opposition to that suppression.

death-penalty.rationale: His programme demanded execution for those responsible for workers’ systematic deprivation.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: He recognised Soviet coercion’s industrial necessity, expressly distinguishing understanding from moral justification.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: He urged substantial American transfers to raise worldwide living standards.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: He accepted economic conditioning of social and political structures, while insisting psychological and sacred forces require their own explanation.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: He distinguished Soviet and Nazi aims despite shared repression.

defeat-communism.rationale: He held that the USSR's tension is of crucial value and that a dynamic peace, not a war to defeat it, is the way; he also hoped the American approach would succeed without war.

alienated-labor.rationale: He described bourgeois production as reducing people to things.

reification.rationale: His analysis treats productive calculation as a system of things that absorbs people; later sovereignty opposes this subordination.

spiritual-nature.rationale: In 'The Sacred Conspiracy' he writes that those starting it are ferociously religious and that mere political activity leaves a void.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: He favoured international allocation by need over creditors’ isolated profits.

smash-state-machine.rationale: His 1935-36 Contre-Attaque texts called for armed revolution, but by 1949 (The Accursed Share) he looked to peaceful evolution; the later view does not settle this statement, so under the recency rule it is left null.

sacred-nation.rationale: In 'Propositions' (1937) he treats the nation as sovereignty demanding inalterability and denying death, which he opposes; the 1935 texts reject the fatherland.

race-social-construct.rationale: In his fascism essay he states that the conception of race lacks an objective base but is subjectively grounded.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: The Contre-Attaque tract at which he spoke says that whoever admits the fatherland betrays, because it turns workers' labour into cannons; 'La patrie ou la Terre' rejects national feeling.

censor-art.rationale: Rests only on a secondary account of his testimony at the Sade trial.

notes:
The early jointly led programme and later peaceful economic strategy are distinguished; conflicting positions remain mixed. Soviet coercion is analysed with explicit moral reservations. Descriptions of fascism and feudal sovereignty are not endorsements. Economic limits to growth do not establish environmentalist policy. Sacred experience does not imply clerical government, and fictional sexual violence does not establish criminal-law positions. All statements were reviewed; no historical inferences were required.

claude-sonnet-5-5 notes: Independent second pass. Searched his own texts: Contre-Attaque manifesto and Cahiers (1935-36), Visions of Excess (Notion of Expenditure, Psychological Structure of Fascism, Popular Front in the Street, Sacred Conspiracy, Nietzsche and the Fascists, Propositions, Use Value of Sade), The Accursed Share vol. I (full text) and vols. II-III (skimmed; the scan is garbled, so none of it is cited). Not obtained: Eroticism, Literature and Evil, Inner Experience, On Nietzsche and the Oeuvres completes (lending-only or unavailable). Government, world and liberty themes are thin because he wrote little on institutions or foreign policy beyond 1935-36 and the Marshall Plan chapter. His views shifted from armed revolution (1935-36) to peaceful evolution (1949); answers use the later statement where it clearly addresses the question. The Psychological Structure of Fascism and Propositions describe fascism and sovereignty analytically and are not used as endorsements.
